title: The Discourse on the Mount of Olives
lead: Jesus' last long teaching in the Synoptic Gospels, given to his disciples on the Mount of Olives across from the Temple (Matthew 24–25; Mark 13; Luke 21:5–36). It begins with his prediction that the Temple will be torn down and answers the question of when, and what sign will mark his coming. Christians read it as fulfilled in the Roman war of AD 66–70, as a prophecy of the end of history, or as both.

sections.b: Mark 13 gives the shortest form, Matthew 24–25 the longest, adding parables of waiting and the judgment of the nations. Luke 21:5–36 sets the talk in the Temple courts and speaks openly of Jerusalem "surrounded by armies" (Luke 21:20) where Matthew and Mark speak of "the abomination of desolation." Luke places some of Matthew's sayings elsewhere (Luke 12:35–48; Luke 17:22–37). Revelation shares many of its images: false prophets, war, famine, darkened sun and falling stars, the mourning tribes, the thief, and the wedding.

Partial preterists read most of the discourse as the Jewish war and the fall of the Temple in AD 70, within "this generation"; full preterists read all of it that way. Futurists read it as a future tribulation and Christ's visible return; dispensationalists center it on Israel after the church is taken up. Historicists trace its signs across church history. Idealists hear it as the pattern of every age: deceivers, suffering and the call to hold out. Many read a near fulfillment in AD 70 that foreshadows the end. Since Albert Schweitzer many historians have held that Jesus or the early church expected the end within a lifetime. All agree that its main command is to stay awake and be ready.
